etymology: From the Latin despicere, to look down upon — de, down, and specere, to look — through the Old French despit. As a noun, contempt shown; an act of open scorn, not merely an inward disdain.
biblical_def: Despite as the Authorized Version uses it is contempt in action, and its gravest occurrence is one of the most solemn sentences in the New Testament: “Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?” (Heb 10:29). Three acts are named in ascending order, and each involves the deliberate contempt of something precious: trampling the Son, reckoning the covenant blood common, and insulting the Spirit of grace. Note the particular name given to the Third Person there — not the Spirit of power or of judgment, but of grace. The offence is not resisting a threat but insulting a kindness, which is why it is the sorest. Ezekiel uses the word of Ammon gloating over Judah’s fall: “thou hast clapped thine hands, and stamped with the feet, and rejoiced in heart with all thy despite against the land of Israel” (Eze 25:6) — contempt so full it required the whole body to express it. And Nehemiah records the same spirit aimed at builders: we are despised, he prays, and turns their reproach upon their own head (Neh 4:4). Despite is always visible. It has to be performed.
webster_summary: Contempt shown or acted out; open scorn and insult, as distinguished from mere inward disdain.
webster_full: DESPITE, n. Extreme malice; violent hatred; malignity; contemptuous defiance.
An act of contempt or malice; injury done in scorn.
From the Latin despicere, to look down upon, from de and specere, to look.
To do despite is to treat with open contumely (Heb 10:29).
Also used adverbially in the phrase in despite of, in contempt or defiance of.
scriptures: Neh 4:4
Hear, O our God; for we are despised: and turn their reproach upon their own head, and give them for a prey in the land of captivity:
Eze 25:6
For thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thou hast clapped thine hands, and stamped with the feet, and rejoiced in heart with all thy despite against the land of Israel;

Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?
It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
corruption_summary: The doctrine of degrees of punishment is largely forgotten, so Hebrews’ warning that some guilt is sorer than other guilt — and that contempt of grace is the sorest — goes unheard.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the flattening of guilt. Two opposite errors produce it. The first supposes all sins are equal, so that no sin can be more dangerous than another and the warnings of Hebrews have nothing particular to say; the second supposes no sin is finally serious, so the warnings have nothing to say at all. Scripture holds neither. It teaches that all sin deserves God’s wrath, and that some sins, by reason of aggravations, are more heinous than others — which is exactly what Heb 10:29 argues. How much sorer punishment is a comparative, and the comparison is with the man who despised Moses’ law and died without mercy under two or three witnesses.

Recover the plain sense: what aggravates guilt here is light received and privilege trampled. The man in view is not an ignorant pagan but one who stood near the blood of the covenant and reckoned it common. That is a warning aimed squarely at the churched, the catechised, and the long-professing, and it is meant to be felt rather than defused. Yet notice where the writer goes next. Having said it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb 10:31), he immediately reminds them of their former days, when they endured a great fight of afflictions, and urges them not to cast away their confidence. The warning is not despair; it is a hand on the shoulder of people in danger of drifting, and the drift it fears is not blasphemy but slow contempt for what was once precious.
roots_summary: Latin despicere, to look down upon — contempt performed; and in Hebrews, insult offered to the Spirit of grace.
roots_lines: Despite — Latin de + specere, to look down upon.
Contempt acted out, not merely felt; it must be performed to be despite.
Eze 25:6: clapping, stamping, rejoicing — contempt using the whole body.
Heb 10:29 names three ascending acts against Son, blood, and Spirit.
The title used is the Spirit of grace — the insult is offered to a kindness.
usage: Heb 10:29 is a comparative: some guilt is sorer by reason of light received.
The warning is aimed at the long-professing, not the ignorant.
Its purpose is to arrest a drift, not to drive to despair (Heb 10:32–35).

etymology: From the Latin exigere, to drive out, demand, or require — ex, out, and agere, to drive. An exactor is one who demands payment by force: a tax-farmer, driver, or oppressor who extracts what is owed and more.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, in one of the most beautiful promises in Isaiah: “For brass I will bring gold, and for iron I will bring silver, and for wood brass, and for stones iron: I will also make thy officers peace, and thine exactors righteousness” (Isa 60:17). The verse works by a series of upgrades — every material replaced by one of greater worth, brass for wood, gold for brass — and then, having established the pattern, Isaiah applies it to government. The officers shall be peace and the exactors righteousness. He does not say the exactors will be abolished; he says they will be transformed into the very thing they usually destroy. That is a remarkable promise, because the exactor is the figure everyone under an ancient empire feared: the man with authority to take, whose visit meant loss. Isaiah announces a government whose collectors are righteousness itself. The following verse completes the picture: “Violence shall no more be heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction within thy borders; but thou shalt call thy walls Salvation, and thy gates Praise” (Isa 60:18). Not merely peaceful walls but walls named Salvation; not merely open gates but gates called Praise. This is not the abolition of order but its healing — authority restored to what God made it for.
webster_summary: Those who demand payment by force — tax-gatherers, drivers, oppressors; in Isa 60:17, the officers whom God promises to transform into righteousness itself.
webster_full: EXACTOR, n. One who exacts; an officer who collects tribute, taxes, or customs with rigour.
An extortioner; one who compels another to pay more than is due.
From the Latin exigere, to drive out, to demand, from ex and agere, to drive.
Isa 60:17: thine exactors righteousness — the office transformed, not abolished.
The Hebrew is elsewhere rendered taskmaster and oppressor.
scriptures: For brass I will bring gold, and for iron I will bring silver, and for wood brass, and for stones iron: I will also make thy officers peace, and thine exactors righteousness.
Violence shall no more be heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction within thy borders; but thou shalt call thy walls Salvation, and thy gates Praise.
The sun shall be no more thy light by day; neither for brightness shall the moon give light unto thee: but the LORD shall be unto thee an everlasting light, and thy God thy glory.
And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof.
corruption_summary: Hope for public life swings between abolishing authority and idolising it, where Isaiah promises neither anarchy nor a strong man but offices healed into peace and righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption runs in two directions, and Isaiah rebukes both. On one side is the utopian instinct that identifies authority itself as the problem, so that the good future is imagined as a world without officers, taxes, or magistrates. On the other is the reflex that idolises office — the strong ruler who will set matters right, before whom criticism becomes disloyalty. Isa 60:17 grants neither wish. The officers remain and the exactors remain; what changes is what they are. Government is not treated as an evil to be escaped nor as a saviour to be trusted, but as a good thing currently corrupted, which God intends to heal.

Recover the plain sense: authority is God’s ordinance and its abuse is the corruption of something originally good. The magistrate is the minister of God to thee for good; that is Paul’s judgment about a Roman empire that would shortly kill him. So the Christian neither despises office nor worships it, but prays for kings and all that are in authority, obeys where he lawfully may, and looks for the day when the collector at the door is righteousness. And notice where Isaiah’s chapter ends up, because the promise is finally not political at all: the sun shall be no more thy light by day, but the LORD shall be unto thee an everlasting light (Isa 60:19) — a sentence John takes up over the city that has no need of the sun, for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof.
roots_summary: Latin exigere, to drive out or demand — the forceful collector; promised in Isaiah to be transformed into righteousness.
roots_lines: Exactors — Latin ex + agere, to drive out, to demand.
One who collects tribute with rigour; a taskmaster or oppressor.
Isa 60:17 upgrades every material: wood to brass, brass to gold.
Then applies the pattern to office: officers peace, exactors righteousness.
Isa 60:18: walls called Salvation, and gates called Praise.
usage: The exactors are not abolished but transformed — office healed, not removed.
Isaiah’s hope is neither anarchy nor a strong man.
The chapter ends with God Himself as the everlasting light (Isa 60:19).

etymology: From the Saxon nawiht — na, no, and wiht, a thing, whence whit: literally no thing, nothing. As an adjective in the Authorized Version it means bad, worthless, good for nothing.
biblical_def: Naught means worthless, and its two occurrences show a bad thing healed and a good thing slandered. At Jericho the men of the city said to Elisha, “the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord seeth: but the water is naught, and the ground barren” (2Ki 2:19). A fine site with a bad spring — everything right except the one thing everything depends on. Elisha called for a new cruse with salt in it, cast it into the spring, and said, “Thus saith the LORD, I have healed these waters” (2Ki 2:21), and the waters were healed unto this day (2Ki 2:22). Note the method: the cure is applied at the source, not to the fields downstream, and the agent is salt, which of itself makes water less drinkable. God heals by means that would not work of themselves. The second occurrence is a small masterpiece of observation: “It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth” (Pro 20:14). The buyer disparages the goods to beat the price down, walks away with the bargain, and then brags about what he got. Solomon has caught a species of lying so ordinary that most men would not call it lying at all — the deliberate misvaluing of another man’s property in order to acquire it cheaply.
webster_summary: Bad, worthless, good for nothing; literally no thing. Used of Jericho’s spring before Elisha healed it, and of the buyer’s false disparagement of goods.
webster_full: NAUGHT, adj. Bad; worthless; of no value or account.
NAUGHT, n. Nothing; as, to set at naught.
From the Saxon nawiht; na, no, and wiht, a thing, a whit.
Distinguished in modern usage from nought, the cipher or zero.
2Ki 2:19: the water is naught — bad, unwholesome.
scriptures: And the men of the city said unto Elisha, Behold, I pray thee, the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord seeth: but the water is naught, and the ground barren.
And he went forth unto the spring of the waters, and cast the salt in there, and said, Thus saith the LORD, I have healed these waters; there shall not be from thence any more death or barren land.
So the waters were healed unto this day, according to the saying of Elisha which he spake.
It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth.
corruption_summary: Hard bargaining by misrepresentation is treated as a skill rather than a lie, though Pro 20:14 catches the buyer disparaging what he intends to buy and boasting once he owns it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is negotiation by misrepresentation. Pro 20:14 describes a transaction everyone recognises: the buyer runs down the goods, calls them worthless, secures a low price, leaves, and immediately boasts of the bargain — which proves he never believed his own valuation. Solomon does not moralise; he simply reports it, and the reporting is the indictment. The practice survives untouched in every market, and it is defended as shrewdness, as leverage, as the way business is done. But the ninth commandment governs valuations as much as testimony. A man who says it is naught about a thing he intends to own has borne false witness about his neighbour’s property.

Recover the plain sense: honest dealing does not require a man to pay more than he wishes or to conceal that he wants a lower price. Bargaining is lawful; lying is not, and the line falls exactly where the words stop describing what one believes. Then set beside it the sweeter half of the word. Jericho’s water was genuinely naught — a real defect, honestly reported by the men of the city — and Elisha healed it at the spring. There is a bad valuation that slanders, and there is a true one that names a real fault so it can be dealt with. The first ruins a neighbour; the second is the beginning of every healing, and God’s way of curing a poisoned stream is always to go up to the source.
roots_summary: Saxon nawiht, no thing — worthless; Jericho’s bad spring healed at its source, and the buyer’s lying valuation.
roots_lines: Naught — Saxon nawiht: na, no, and wiht, a thing.
The same wiht gives English whit, as in not a whit.
As an adjective in the AV it means bad or worthless, not merely absent.
2Ki 2:21: the cure is cast into the spring, not spread on the fields.
Salt of itself spoils water — God heals by means that would not work alone.
usage: Pro 20:14: the boast afterwards proves the disparagement was a lie.
The ninth commandment governs valuations as well as testimony.
Elisha treats the source; a poisoned spring is never cured downstream.

etymology: From the Latin delectabilis, delightful, from delectare, to delight — the root of delight itself. That which gives pleasure; highly pleasing to the senses or the affections.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, and its setting is Isaiah’s great satire on idolatry: “They that make a graven image are all of them vanity; and their delectable things shall not profit; and they are their own witnesses; they see not, nor know; that they may be ashamed” (Isa 44:9). The choice of adjective is exact and merciless. Isaiah does not call the idols hideous or absurd; he calls them delectable — delightful, genuinely pleasing. That is the whole trouble with them. The chapter that follows contains the most devastating description of idol-making in Scripture: a man plants an ash, the rain nourishes it, he burns half of it to warm himself and bake his bread, roasts his meat and is satisfied, and of the residue he makes a god and falls down to it, saying Deliver me; for thou art my god. And the prophet’s verdict is not that the man is stupid but that a deceived heart hath turned him aside. Note the two things Isaiah asserts together in verse 9. The idols are genuinely delightful, and they shall not profit. The question was never whether an idol gives pleasure; it is whether it delivers. “Who hath formed a god, or molten a graven image that is profitable for nothing?” (Isa 44:10) — the answer being, a great many people, and cheerfully.
webster_summary: Delightful; highly pleasing to the senses or affections. Isaiah’s word for idols — genuinely pleasant, and wholly unable to profit.
webster_full: DELECTABLE, adj. Pleasing; delightful; highly agreeable.
From the Latin delectabilis, from delectare, to delight.
Of the same family as delight, delectation, and dilettante.
Applied to whatever gratifies the senses or the affections.
Isa 44:9: the idolater’s delectable things which shall not profit.
scriptures: Isa 44:9
They that make a graven image are all of them vanity; and their delectable things shall not profit; and they are their own witnesses; they see not, nor know; that they may be ashamed.
Who hath formed a god, or molten a graven image that is profitable for nothing?
He feedeth on ashes: a deceived heart hath turned him aside, that he cannot deliver his soul, nor say, Is there not a lie in my right hand?
Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as the worship of obviously ridiculous objects by primitive people, when Isaiah’s word for idols is delectable — they are chosen precisely because they delight.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the museum view of idolatry. Because the idols named in Scripture are carved images, modern readers file the sin under ancient superstition and conclude that it has no purchase on a society that keeps no household gods. Isaiah’s adjective forbids the comfort. The things men make into gods are delectable — genuinely lovely, satisfying, and worth having, which is exactly why they are chosen. Nobody ever worshipped something he found dull. The modern forms are correspondingly attractive: work that gives a man his identity, a family made the whole reason for living, comfort, security, reputation, a cause. Each is a real good, and each is a delectable thing that shall not profit when it is asked to do what only God can do.

Recover the plain sense: the test Isaiah applies is not attractiveness but profit. Can it deliver? The man in Isa 44 warms himself at half his tree and prays to the other half, and the prophet says he feedeth on ashes: a deceived heart hath turned him aside, that he cannot deliver his soul, nor say, Is there not a lie in my right hand? (Isa 44:20). That last question is the one every idolater is unable to ask himself, which is why idolatry is so nearly invisible from the inside. Jeremiah supplies the plainest statement of the whole matter: God’s people committed two evils — they forsook the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water (Jer 2:13). The cistern was a good idea. It was simply not a fountain.
roots_summary: Latin delectare, to delight — delightful; Isaiah’s word for idols that genuinely please and cannot profit.
roots_lines: Delectable — Latin delectabilis, from delectare, to delight.
Kin to delight and delectation.
Isa 44:9 calls the idols delightful, not ridiculous — that is the trouble.
Isa 44:20: he feedeth on ashes: a deceived heart hath turned him aside.
Jer 2:13: broken cisterns forsaking the fountain of living waters.
usage: Nobody worships what he finds dull; idols are chosen because they please.
Isaiah’s test is not attractiveness but profit — can it deliver?
Is there not a lie in my right hand? is the question idolatry cannot ask itself.

etymology: From the Latin durare, to last or harden, from durus, hard — the root of endure and duration. That which lasts; capable of continuing long without perishing.
biblical_def: Durable is Wisdom’s adjective for the only riches worth the name: “Riches and honour are with me; yea, durable riches and righteousness” (Pro 8:18). The whole force lies in the qualifier. Wisdom does not deny that riches exist elsewhere; she claims that hers last, and the pairing with righteousness is deliberate, since it is righteousness that makes wealth durable. Riches gotten by vanity shall be diminished; treasures of wickedness profit nothing; the rich man’s wealth is his strong city and as an high wall in his own conceit. Solomon presses the comparison in the next verse: “My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver” (Pro 8:19). Isaiah takes the same word into an unexpected place. Of Tyre, the great trading city under judgment, he prophesies that at length “her merchandise and her hire shall be holiness to the LORD: it shall not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the LORD, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing” (Isa 23:18). Tyre’s commerce, once the byword for pride, becomes provision for God’s people — food enough and clothing that lasts — and the text specifies that it shall not be treasured nor laid up. Durable wealth is defined here as wealth that is spent well, not hoarded.
webster_summary: Lasting; able to continue long without perishing. Applied to Wisdom’s riches, which endure because they are joined to righteousness.
webster_full: DURABLE, adj. Having the quality of lasting or continuing long in being.
Not perishable or changeable; permanent; as durable riches.
From the Latin durare, to last, from durus, hard.
Of the same family as endure, duration, and obdurate.
Pro 8:18: durable riches and righteousness — the two joined.
scriptures: Pro 8:18
Riches and honour are with me; yea, durable riches and righteousness.
Pro 8:19
My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver.

And her merchandise and her hire shall be holiness to the LORD: it shall not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the LORD, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing.
Mat 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
corruption_summary: Wealth is measured by accumulation, where Scripture measures it by duration — and Isa 23:18 defines durable provision as what is spent well rather than treasured up.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the confusion of quantity with permanence. A man asks how much have I, and Scripture asks how long will it last, and the two questions produce very different lives. Proverbs is not ascetic; it says frankly that riches and honour are with Wisdom, and that her fruit is better than fine gold. But the adjective it attaches is durable, and the noun it pairs with is righteousness, because unrighteous wealth is by nature temporary — it must be defended, it decays in the keeping, and it cannot be carried past the grave. James saw the gold of the hoarders cankered in their own vaults.

Recover the plain sense: our Lord gives the practical instruction that follows from the doctrine — lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal (Mat 6:20). He does not forbid treasure; He relocates it to the one vault with no moth, no rust, and no thief. Isaiah shows what that looks like in practice, and it is startling: Tyre’s merchandise becomes holiness to the LORD precisely by not being treasured or laid up, going instead to feed those who dwell before the LORD and to clothe them durably. Wealth becomes permanent at the moment it is spent on what is permanent. That is the arithmetic of the kingdom, and it is exactly backwards from the world’s.
roots_summary: Latin durare, to last — enduring; Wisdom’s riches, durable because joined to righteousness and spent rather than hoarded.
roots_lines: Durable — Latin durare, to last, from durus, hard.
Kin to endure, duration, and obdurate.
Pro 8:18 joins durable riches to righteousness — the two are not separable.
Isa 23:18: durable clothing, from merchandise not treasured nor laid up.
Mat 6:20 relocates treasure to the vault with no moth, rust, or thief.
usage: Scripture measures wealth by duration, not by quantity.
Isa 23:18 makes provision durable precisely by not hoarding it.
Proverbs is not ascetic — riches and honour are with Wisdom.

etymology: Rendering the Hebrew tardemah, a heavy, God-sent trance or stupor — from a root meaning to be fast asleep. It is never ordinary slumber in Scripture but a sleep imposed, and always at a moment of consequence.
biblical_def: Deep sleep renders the Hebrew tardemah, and it is never simple tiredness. It is a sleep God causes, and it falls at the hinges of redemptive history. It falls on Adam when the woman is made: “the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs” (Gen 2:21) — the man is unconscious while his bride is formed from his opened side, and he wakes to receive her. It falls on Abram when the covenant is cut: “when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and, lo, an horror of great darkness fell upon him” (Gen 15:12), and while he sleeps a smoking furnace and a burning lamp pass between the pieces alone. Abram does not walk the covenant path; God binds Himself while the man lies senseless. It falls on Saul’s camp so that David may take the spear and the cruse: “no man saw it, nor knew it, neither awaked: for they were all asleep; because a deep sleep from the LORD was fallen upon them” (1Sa 26:12). And it falls in judgment, when God pours out “the spirit of deep sleep” on prophets and seers who would not see (Isa 29:10). Elihu adds that God speaks in dreams “when deep sleep falleth upon men” (Job 33:15). In every case the sleeper contributes nothing. That is the doctrine.
webster_summary: The Hebrew tardemah: a heavy, God-imposed sleep or trance, falling at moments of covenant, creation, deliverance, and judgment.
webster_full: DEEP SLEEP, the rendering of the Hebrew tardemah, a profound sleep or trance.
Distinguished from ordinary slumber; always imposed rather than merely fallen into.
Sent for creation (Gen 2:21) and for covenant (Gen 15:12).
Sent for deliverance, as upon Saul’s camp (1Sa 26:12).
Sent in judgment, as the spirit of deep sleep upon prophets and seers (Isa 29:10).
scriptures: Gen 2:21
And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof;
And when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and, lo, an horror of great darkness fell upon him.

So David took the spear and the cruse of water from Saul's bolster; and they gat them away, and no man saw it, nor knew it, neither awaked: for they were all asleep; because a deep sleep from the LORD was fallen upon them.
For the LORD hath poured out upon you the spirit of deep sleep, and hath closed your eyes: the prophets and your rulers, the seers hath he covered.
corruption_summary: Salvation is increasingly described as a decision the sinner contributes, where every tardemah in Scripture shows the decisive work done while the man lies wholly passive.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the doctrine of the contributing sinner. Modern evangelism frequently presents salvation as a transaction in which God supplies the offer and the man supplies the decision, so that the deciding is the hinge on which everything turns. The tardemah passages are a standing rebuke to that scheme. At the making of the bride, Adam is asleep; at the cutting of the covenant, Abram is asleep and a horror of great darkness is upon him, and the furnace and the lamp pass between the pieces without him. In the ancient rite, both parties walked the bloody path to say so be it done to me if I break this. God walked it alone. The covenant was made unilaterally over an unconscious man.

Recover the plain sense: this is why the confessions speak of a man dead in trespasses and sins being quickened, not assisted — the deep sleep of nature, as the older writers called it, from which no man wakes himself. And the typology is too exact to be accidental. A deep sleep falls on the first Adam, his side is opened, and from it a bride is built; a sleep of death falls on the last Adam, His side is opened by a spear, and from it His bride is formed. In neither case does the bride contribute to her own making. Note finally the sobering use in Isa 29:10: God may also send such a sleep in judgment upon those who have long refused to see. The same hand that puts a man to sleep to save him can close the eyes of a prophet who would not use them.
roots_summary: Hebrew tardemah, a God-sent trance — falling at creation, covenant, deliverance, and judgment; the sleeper contributes nothing.
roots_lines: Deep sleep — Hebrew tardemah, a heavy, imposed sleep or trance.
Never ordinary tiredness; always sent, and always at a moment of consequence.
Gen 2:21: the bride formed from the opened side of a sleeping man.
Gen 15:12: God alone passes between the pieces while Abram sleeps.
Isa 29:10: the spirit of deep sleep poured out in judgment on seers.
usage: In every instance the sleeper contributes nothing to what is done.
Gen 15 is a unilateral covenant — only God walks between the pieces.
First Adam asleep, side opened, bride built; last Adam likewise.
